report:
**Conclusion: You are correct — regular vitamin C intake does not prevent colds in the general population.**

The most authoritative evidence comes from the **Cochrane systematic review** by Hemilä and Chalker, which analyzed 29 trial comparisons involving 11,306 participants. It found that regular vitamin C supplementation (≥200 mg/day) did **not** reduce the incidence of colds in the general population. For the average person, taking vitamin C daily neither prevents catching a cold nor meaningfully reduces how often one occurs ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold)).

**One important exception:** In five trials involving 598 participants under **short periods of extreme physical stress** (marathon runners, skiers, soldiers in sub-arctic conditions), vitamin C supplementation **did** halve the incidence of colds ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold); [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/)). This benefit appears limited to people subjected to acute physical exertion and does not extend to the general public.

**However, vitamin C is not without any benefit:** A 2023 meta-analysis found that while vitamin C doesn't prevent colds, regular supplementation can modestly **reduce the duration and severity** of colds that do occur, particularly for severe symptoms ([Springer/BMC Public Health](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8)). The Cochrane review similarly noted a slight reduction in cold duration (about 8% in adults, 14% in children).

**Bottom line:** For prevention of colds in ordinary people, the answer is **no** — vitamin C won't stop you from getting sick. It may slightly shorten colds once you have them, and it may help prevent colds in people under extreme physical stress, but for the general population, the preventive benefit is absent ([MDEdge](https://mdedge.com/familymedicine/article/270936/infectious-diseases/myth-month-vitamin-c-vs-common-cold)).
